text_kjv: He will swallow up death in victory; and the Lord GOD will wipe away tears from off all faces; and the rebuke of his people shall he take away from off all the earth: for the LORD hath spoken it.

commentary.narrative:
This is one of the most luminous prophecies in all of Isaiah—a declaration of ultimate triumph over death itself. Written in the context of Isaiah's apocalyptic vision of the end times, this verse stands as the climax of a section that begins with the destruction of the enemies of God's people and culminates in the complete reversal of all suffering and shame. The prophet uses visceral language: death is not merely conquered, but 'swallowed up'—absorbed, consumed, annihilated. The image of God wiping tears from every face speaks to the totality of redemption: not just spiritual salvation, but the healing of every wound, the answer to every grief, the vindication of every soul who has suffered under the weight of mortality and sin.

For Isaiah's original audience, exiled and oppressed, this was a word of eschatological hope. But for the Latter-day Saint reader, this verse becomes clarified and amplified through the Restoration. We know, through modern revelation, that death has been overcome through the Atonement and Resurrection of Jesus Christ—and we also know that the 'rebuke' that is taken away includes the shame that death brought upon humanity through the Fall. The verse announces not mere rescue but complete vindication: the reversal of every consequence of the Fall except for those that serve our eternal progression.

The phrase 'for the LORD hath spoken it' anchors the entire promise in the unbreakable word of God. This is not wishful speculation or mythological hope; it is the covenant word of Jehovah, binding and eternal. In the context of Easter—the historical moment when death's victory was broken—this verse becomes the scriptural lens through which we understand what Christ's Resurrection means for all of God's children. Every tear shed in mortality will be accounted for. Every death will be swallowed up in victory.

word_study.meaning: to swallow, consume, devour; to absorb completely; used of the earth swallowing the wicked (Numbers 16:32) and of the flood consuming the land (Genesis 7:23). The piel form (intensive) suggests not mere removal but utter annihilation and incorporation.
word_study.significance: The choice of this verb is deliberate and violent—not a gentle passing away, but death itself consumed by a greater force. In the context of Easter, this captures the total victory of Christ's Resurrection: death is not simply left behind or transcended; it is swallowed, consumed, made null.

word_study.meaning: victory, triumph, eternity, perpetuity. Can also mean 'brightness' or 'splendor.' The root suggests permanence and superiority.
word_study.significance: This is not a temporary reprieve from death but a permanent, eternal victory. The word's association with eternity suggests that this triumph transcends mortality itself—it is forever.

word_study.meaning: to wipe away, erase, blot out, remove. Used of God blotting out sin (Isaiah 43:25) and of Moses blotting out names from the Book of Life (Exodus 32:33).
word_study.significance: The act of wiping away tears is not passive comfort but active divine erasure—God Himself removes the cause and evidence of grief. This speaks to God's personal, intimate involvement in healing.

word_study.meaning: reproach, shame, disgrace, insult. Often used of the shame Israel experiences under oppression or judgment.
word_study.significance: In the context of death and the Fall, this 'rebuke' may refer to the shame and humiliation that mortality brought upon humanity—the diminishment of being subject to death. The removal of this rebuke suggests not just escape from death but restoration of dignity and honor.

cross_references.connection: Paul directly quotes Isaiah 25:8 ('Death is swallowed up in victory') as the fulfillment of Christ's victory over death through the Resurrection, making explicit what Isaiah prophesied.

John's vision of the new creation echoes Isaiah 25:8: 'And God shall wipe away all tears from their eyes; and there shall be no more death.' This shows the eschatological completion of Isaiah's prophecy at the end of all things.
The Book of Mormon quotes Isaiah 25:8 in full as part of the Abinadi prophecy, applying it directly to Christ's victory and the redemption of mankind.

The Lord promises the Saints: 'Therefore, fear not, little flock; do good; let earth and hell combine against you, for if ye are built upon my rock, they cannot prevail.' This echoes Isaiah's promise that God's people will be vindicated and delivered from their 'rebuke.'
In Nephi's quotation of Isaiah material, this verse frames the larger context of covenant salvation and the removal of shame from God's people.

commentary.historical_context:
Isaiah 25 is part of Isaiah's apocalyptic vision known as the 'Isaiah Apocalypse' (chapters 24-27). It follows a dramatic description of judgment on 'the city' (likely referring to the enemies of Israel and the corrupt systems of the world) and precedes a celebration of God's protection of Mount Zion. In the historical context of Isaiah's ministry (likely 8th century BCE, though some scholars date this section later), the people of Judah faced the threat of Assyrian invasion and exile. The promise of death being swallowed up would have offered profound eschatological hope—not merely political deliverance, but cosmic redemption.

Ancient Near Eastern funeral practices and the culture of lament were central to the world Isaiah addressed. Mourning rituals were elaborate and prolonged. The image of God wiping away tears would resonate as an act of supreme compassion and power—only a god could reverse the necessities of death and grief. The 'rebuke' of a people was a tangible cultural shame that affected social standing and covenant status. For Isaiah to promise its removal was to promise complete restoration to favor and honor.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Abinadi quotes Isaiah 25:8 in full in Mosiah 14:8, directly applying it to Christ's Atonement and Resurrection. This shows that the Book of Mormon understood this passage as directly Christological—not merely an abstract eschatological promise, but the specific work of the Savior. The Nephite prophets understood that the 'victory' over death would come through a specific person and event: the Savior's Resurrection.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: In D&C 76:39, Joseph Smith records that those who inherit the celestial kingdom will 'be heirs of God and joint-heirs with Jesus Christ.' This doctrine of exaltation and inherited glory is the fulfillment of Isaiah's promise that God's people will have the 'rebuke' taken away—they will be vindicated and exalted. Additionally, D&C 19:6 affirms that Christ's Atonement extends to all humanity: 'Wherefore, I command you again to repent, lest I humble you with my almightiness.' The victory over death is offered to all who come unto Christ.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The imagery of tears being wiped away and rebuke removed echoes the temple experience of being restored to the presence of God and to covenant standing. In the temple, we experience the reversal of the Fall: the removal of shame (represented by fig leaves), the restoration of communication with God (through the veil), and the promise of exaltation. The 'swallowing up of death in victory' is the ultimate fruit of temple covenants—eternal life in the presence of God.

commentary.christological_typology: This verse is not typological in the traditional sense (where a person or object prefigures Christ) but is explicitly Messianic prophecy. The one who 'swallows up death in victory' is Christ Himself. The Resurrection of Jesus Christ is the singular historical event that fulfills this prophecy. Through His Atonement and Resurrection, Christ conquered death—not merely for Himself, but for all humanity. Paul's quotation in 1 Corinthians 15:54-55 makes this connection explicit: the victory over death that Isaiah prophesied is won through Christ's triumph. The 'rebuke' that is removed can also be understood as the shame and condemnation that sin brought upon humanity; Christ's Atonement removes this shame from all who come unto Him. The image of God wiping away tears points to Christ's compassion and the intimate knowledge He has of human suffering—He wept at the tomb of Lazarus (John 11:35), demonstrating His perfect empathy with human grief, even as He possesses the power to reverse it eternally.
commentary.application: For modern covenant members, Isaiah 25:8 is a promise that anchors faith in Christ's Resurrection beyond abstract theology into concrete hope about our own mortality and grief. Every tear shed in this life—over loss, illness, heartbreak, injustice—is seen and accounted for by God. The Atonement and Resurrection of Christ mean that no grief is wasted and no suffering is meaningless. In the resurrection, all will be redeemed: the widow will see her spouse again, the parent will embrace the lost child, every relationship severed by death will be restored. The 'rebuke' that is removed speaks to the vindication of the righteous: those who have endured persecution, shame, or diminishment in this life will be exalted and honored in the life to come. This verse calls us to view mortality not as the final word but as a temporary condition whose power has already been broken by Christ. It invites us to mourn with those who mourn (knowing that grief is honored), but also to testify with conviction that death does not have the last word.

text_kjv: And it shall be said in that day, Lo, this is our God; we have waited for him, and he will save us: this is the LORD; we have waited for him, we will be glad and rejoice in his salvation.

commentary.narrative:
If Isaiah 25:8 is the prophecy of what God will do, then Isaiah 25:9 is the response of God's people when that prophecy is fulfilled. The verse shifts from the cosmic declaration of victory to the personal testimony and rejoicing of those who have waited for the Lord's salvation. The repetition of 'we have waited for him' frames the entire history of covenant Israel—and by extension, the entire covenant people of God across all ages—as one long waiting, one extended expression of faith and hope in the promises of God. The phrase 'Lo, this is our God' is a recognition, a moment of clarity in which the people finally see with unveiled eyes that the One they have been waiting for is indeed the God of their covenant, the Keeper of His word.

This verse moves from the personal to the communal, from the individual testimony to the unified voice of God's people. The phrase 'we have waited,' repeated twice in parallel structure, emphasizes the constancy of Israel's faith across generations—through exile, oppression, and longing. But waiting here is not passive; it is the active maintenance of covenant faith, the refusal to abandon hope in God's promises. When the prophecy is fulfilled—when death is swallowed up and tears are wiped away—the response is unstoppable joy. 'We will be glad and rejoice in his salvation' uses the strongest language of celebration: not mere contentment, but exultation, dancing, shouts of joy.

For the Latter-day Saint reader, this verse carries profound weight because we are literally living in the era when these promises are being fulfilled. We have the testimony of the Resurrection; we know that Christ has conquered death; we await the resurrection of the dead. When we say 'we have waited for him,' we are joining our voices to the cloud of witnesses across all dispensations who have held onto this hope. The verse invites us to recognize that what we celebrate on Easter—the triumph of Christ—is the direct answer to the ancient prayers and hopes of all the faithful across time.

word_study.meaning: to wait, to hope, to look forward to; can also mean 'to bind together' (a string pulled taut). The root suggests both temporal waiting and the emotional state of expectation.
word_study.significance: This is not mere passive waiting but active maintenance of hope and faith. The people are held in a state of tension and expectation, bound together by their shared hope in God's promise. The repetition of this word in one verse emphasizes both the length of the waiting and its unbroken continuity.

word_study.meaning: to save, deliver, help, rescue; broadly, to vindicate and restore to wholeness. The root can also mean 'to be wide/spacious,' suggesting the idea of moving from constriction to freedom.
word_study.significance: Salvation in Isaiah is not purely spiritual but encompasses physical deliverance, healing, and restoration. It is the reversal of all that has diminished or oppressed God's people—including the ultimate oppression of death itself.

word_study.meaning: to be glad, to rejoice, to be joyful; can indicate both inward emotion and outward expression of joy.
word_study.significance: This is the joy of deliverance, the emotional response to salvation realized. It is not quiet contentment but expressive, celebratory joy.

word_study.meaning: to rejoice, to exult, to tremble with joy; suggests intense, almost overwhelming emotion.
word_study.significance: This verb intensifies the emotion beyond 'gladness'—it is exultation, the kind of joy that shakes the body and cannot be contained. The doubling of 'glad and rejoice' creates a crescendo of emotion.

cross_references.connection: This is the Lord's day; we will be glad and rejoice in it.' Isaiah 25:9 echoes this psalm's celebration of God's salvation, making clear that the rejoicing of God's people is a constant refrain throughout scripture.

Peter declares that Christians are 'begotten again unto a lively hope by the resurrection of Jesus Christ from the dead' and rejoice with 'joy unspeakable.' This is the direct New Testament fulfillment of Isaiah's promise of glad rejoicing in the salvation of God.

Joseph F. Smith's vision of the spirit world reveals that the faithful have been waiting in the paradise of God, holding fast to their faith in Christ's redemption. This is the spiritual context of Isaiah's 'we have waited for him'—the waiting of all the faithful across time for Christ's ultimate victory.

Alma teaches that through the resurrection of Christ, all will be brought to stand before God and be judged. The righteous will 'be glad' in His presence (Alma 12:14). This echoes Isaiah's promise of gladness and rejoicing in salvation.

The marriage supper of the Lamb is announced: 'Let us be glad and rejoice, and give honour to him.' This is the ultimate fulfillment of Isaiah 25:9—the complete gathering of God's people to rejoice in His salvation.

commentary.historical_context:
The historical-cultural background to this verse lies in the ancient practice of testimony and communal witness. When Isaiah says 'it shall be said in that day,' he is envisioning a moment of collective recognition and declaration. In ancient Israel, such moments of communal testimony occurred during covenant renewal ceremonies, during celebrations of deliverance (like Passover), and during gatherings at the temple. The use of 'we' language was central to Israelite identity—they thought of themselves not as isolated individuals but as members of a covenanted people with a shared history and destiny.

The concept of waiting had particular resonance in exile or times of oppression. To wait for God while under the dominion of foreign powers or under the threat of destruction required extraordinary faith. The people's willingness to maintain hope across generations—to teach their children to 'wait for him' as they themselves were taught—was an act of spiritual resistance. The joy and rejoicing described in this verse would have been recognized as the natural response to deliverance from bondage, as echoed in the song of the Red Sea (Exodus 15) and in other psalms of deliverance and thanksgiving.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The Book of Mormon frequently emphasizes the waiting of the faithful for Christ. Nephi speaks of his people's expectation of the coming of Christ (1 Nephi 10:4-7), and this waiting is presented as the central hope of the righteous throughout the Nephite dispensation. When Christ appears to the Nephites after His Resurrection, their response mirrors Isaiah 25:9—they recognize Him, they rejoice, and they bear witness: 'Hosanna! Blessed be the name of the Most High God!' (3 Nephi 11:14-16). The Book of Mormon demonstrates the fulfillment of Isaiah's prophecy in miniature: the people have waited for the Savior, and when He manifests Himself, their response is joyful testimony.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 76 presents Joseph Smith's vision of the degrees of glory and reveals the fulfillment of all God's promises of salvation. The doctrine taught there—that all will be raised in the resurrection and that the righteous will inherit glory—is the direct answer to what Isaiah prophesied. Additionally, D&C 128:22-23 teaches that the righteous from all ages will gather in the resurrection and hear the proclamation of their salvation. This is Isaiah's vision made concrete through modern revelation: 'all who have waited for him' will finally see the full realization of their hope.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple is the place where, in types and shadows, we participate in the fulfillment of God's promises. As we pass through the veil in the temple, we approach the presence of God, and the work done there is the work of redemption and salvation. The promise of Isaiah 25:9—that we will say 'this is our God'—is realized in the temple experience, where we come into the presence of God and affirm our covenant relationship with Him. The temple endowment is, in a sense, a rehearsal and preview of the moment described in this verse: the gathering of God's people before Him in joy and recognition.

commentary.christological_typology: While Isaiah 25:9 does not contain typology in the narrow sense, it is directly Christological in content. The one for whom the people have 'waited' is Christ. The salvation in which they 'rejoice' is the salvation won through His Atonement and Resurrection. The entire arc of the Old Testament—from Adam's promise of a Savior (Moses 5:9) through Abraham's covenant (Genesis 12:3) through the Law of Moses (Galatians 3:24) and the prophets—is one long process of God's people waiting for the Messiah. Isaiah's contemporaries did not fully understand that they were waiting specifically for Jesus of Nazareth; they understood it in terms of God's promised King and Deliverer. But the New Testament makes it clear that the fulfillment of this waiting is Christ. The apostle Peter writes that the prophets 'inquired and searched diligently' concerning Christ, seeking 'what manner of time the Spirit of Christ which was in them did signify' (1 Peter 1:10-11). In this sense, every faithful person who 'waited for him' across the ages was waiting specifically for Christ, even if they did not know His name. When Isaiah 25:9 is fully realized, it is in the context of the final resurrection and judgment, when all people will see Christ and be gathered before Him (Revelation 1:7, D&C 88:102-104).
commentary.application: For modern believers, Isaiah 25:9 challenges us to examine the nature of our own waiting. Are we actively maintaining faith in Christ's promises, or have we settled into a passive, cultural Christianity? The verse calls us to a deliberate, intentional hope—we 'wait for him' not out of obligation but out of genuine anticipation of His promised return and the final restoration of all things. It also invites us to join our voices to the communal testimony of the Church: 'we have waited for him.' We are not isolated believers but members of a covenant community that stretches back through all dispensations. When we testify of Christ, when we rejoice in His Atonement and Resurrection, we are joining the ancient chorus of faithful voices who maintained hope across centuries. Finally, the verse calls us to prepare our hearts for gladness and joy. The salvation of Christ is not a heavy, burdensome doctrine but one that should produce in us 'joy unspeakable and full of glory' (1 Peter 1:8). If our faith does not produce gladness and rejoicing, we may need to examine whether we have truly grasped what Isaiah here declares: that we serve a God who has conquered death, who vindicates His people, and who invites us to exult in His salvation.

text_kjv: He is despised and rejected of men; a man of sorrows, and acquainted with grief: and we hid as it were our faces from him; he was despised, and we esteemed him not.

commentary.narrative: This verse marks the nadir of the Suffering Servant's earthly experience—a moment of complete isolation and rejection. Isaiah does not depict the Messiah in glory or majesty, but in profound humiliation. The phrase "despised and rejected of men" uses the plural 'men' to indicate this rejection was universal, not isolated to specific opponents. The Hebrew parallelism (despised/rejected, sorrows/grief) creates a cumulative effect: the Servant's suffering is not merely physical but existential, a complete social and spiritual degradation. When Isaiah says "we hid as it were our faces from him," he captures a visceral response—the inability or unwillingness to look upon his suffering. This is not merely literary description; it reflects an actual historical reality that the disciples would later recognize in Christ's arrest, trial, and crucifixion. For the theme "He Will Swallow Up Death in Victory," this verse establishes the essential contrast: victory emerges only through the depths of defeat. The Messiah must first be utterly rejected and despised before his triumph can have redemptive power. Without this complete descent into human suffering and social death, there is no subsequent victory over actual death.

word_study.meaning: treated as worthless, rejected with contempt. The root בוז (buz) means to despise or treat with disdain. The passive form indicates the Servant is the object of contempt rather than its agent.
word_study.significance: This is not shame the Servant takes upon himself by choice, but contempt forced upon him by others. The passive voice emphasizes victimization and powerlessness in the moment, making the later victory more profound.

word_study.meaning: forsaken, abandoned, or cast off. The sense is of being utterly separated or left without support.
word_study.significance: The Servant experiences not just social rejection but abandonment—a foreshadowing of Christ's cry of dereliction on the cross (Matthew 27:46), which many Latter-day Saints understand as the moment of deepest separation from His Father's presence.

word_study.meaning: to know through intimate experience, not merely intellectual knowledge. Often connotes relational or experiential knowing.
word_study.significance: The Servant does not merely understand grief conceptually; he knows it intimately, through lived experience. This personal familiarity with suffering is essential to his redemptive power—he suffers as humans suffer, not as a detached observer.

cross_references.connection: This is the Book of Mormon's quotation of Isaiah 53:3, brought to the Americas centuries before Christ's mortal ministry, testifying that Nephite prophets understood the Servant's rejection as a fundamental doctrine.
Peter applies Isaiah 53 to Christ's actual suffering and reviling, showing how the apostles recognized the Servant passage as prophecy of Christ's earthly humiliation and its redemptive purpose.

John's prologue echoes the theme of rejection: 'He came unto his own, and his own received him not,' making explicit what Isaiah describes prophetically about the incarnate Word's reception among humanity.

The Lord reveals to Joseph Smith the nature of Christ's Gethsemane suffering: 'sufferings caused myself, even God the greatest of all, to tremble because of pain, and to bleed at every pore.' This illuminates the depth of the Servant's anguish beyond mere social rejection.

commentary.historical_context: In the Ancient Near Eastern royal and royal-servant literature, a figure might be described as humiliated or defeated, but Isaiah 53 is extraordinary in depicting the agent of redemption precisely through his greatest degradation, contrary to every expectation of victory. The Servant is presented as anti-heroic: lowly, suffering, rejected—categories that would have seemed absurd as descriptions of the expected Davidic Messiah in mainstream Jewish expectation. The repeated use of 'we' and 'us' throughout Isaiah 53 indicates communal responsibility for the Servant's suffering; this is not an innocent third party suffering, but one whose suffering is somehow bound up with the sin and condition of the people. The Hebrew concept of corporate solidarity and representative suffering may underlie this passage. Archaeological insight into Second Temple Judaism shows that popular messianic expectations centered on a military or political deliverer; a humiliated, suffering messiah was not part of the standard typology, making this prophecy all the more striking and controversial in later Jewish-Christian debate.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Abinadi (Mosiah 13) explicitly applies the Suffering Servant passage to Jesus Christ, teaching that the law points to the coming Savior who will be 'despised and rejected' despite being 'the light and the life of the world.' Alma 7:11-13 similarly emphasizes that Christ 'shall take upon him the pains and the sicknesses of his people' and 'succor his people according to their infirmities.' These passages show how Nephite and Lamanite prophets understood the Servant's rejection not as tragedy but as essential to the atonement's scope and power.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 38:4 uses Christological language: 'I am the same which have taken the Zion of the Pure in heart,' indicating the Servant's identity and purpose. More directly, D&C 133:50-56 contains a prophecy of Christ's return and vindication, suggesting the theological rhythm of rejection-then-exaltation that Isaiah 53 establishes. The entire D&C emphasis on Christ as the central figure of all dispensations validates Isaiah's depiction of the Servant as the hinge of human history.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The Servant's experience of rejection and bearing of suffering connects to the temple covenant themes of sacrifice and atonement. In the endowment, the initiate enters as the Servant enters—humiliated, stripped of worldly distinctions, brought low—only to be exalted. This mirrors the Servant's pattern. Additionally, the garment worn in the temple inscribes covenants that reference Christ's suffering; members literally clothe themselves in the implications of the Servant's humiliation and glorification.

commentary.christological_typology: Isaiah 53:3 identifies the Servant as the one who fulfills the ultimate typology of redemptive suffering. Whereas Old Testament sacrifices and suffering servants pointed forward to a final redemptive act, this verse identifies that future Servant with a specific person whose character—despised, rejected, acquainted with grief—is central to his work. The rejection is not incidental to his mission; it is essential. Christ's rejection by the Jewish leadership and the Roman state becomes, in this typology, the exact fulfillment of the Servant's role. His weakness (apparent powerlessness before his accusers) is the revelation of his strength (willing submission to the Father's will for humanity's redemption). The Servant's descent into shame precedes and enables his ascent to victory.
commentary.application: For modern covenant members, Isaiah 53:3 teaches a counterintuitive spiritual truth: the path to victory often passes through visible humiliation and rejection. Members who face social marginalization for their faith, or who endure private struggles that make them feel despised or cast out, find profound reassurance that Christ himself was despised and rejected. More deeply, the verse invites introspection about our own role as 'we'—the people who 'hid our faces' from the Servant. This implicates us in the very rejection that Christ endured for us. Repentance, then, is not merely regret but a reorientation toward the one we hid from, an act of turning our faces back toward him. Practically, this verse teaches that faithful living sometimes means accepting rejection and loss of status in the eyes of the world—and that this, far from disproving our faith, may be evidence of its authenticity. The Servant's example sanctifies our suffering and validates our willingness to be despised if it means remaining faithful to the covenant.

text_kjv: Surely he hath borne our griefs, and carried our sorrows: yet we did esteem him stricken, smitten of God, and afflicted.

commentary.narrative: Here Isaiah transitions from describing the Servant's rejection to explaining its meaning: his suffering is redemptive and vicarious. The word "Surely" (Hebrew אַךְ akh) signals an emphatic assertion—what follows is not speculation but certainty. "Hath borne our griefs" uses the language of carrying or sustaining a burden; the Servant absorbs the weight of human suffering into himself. The critical theological move comes in the parenthetical clause: "yet we did esteem him stricken, smitten of God, and afflicted." The human witnesses—the 'we' who speak—misinterpreted the Servant's suffering as divine punishment for his own sin. This is a profound statement about the opacity of suffering: the Servant appears to be cursed by God, when in fact he is bearing the curse that belongs to others. For the Easter theme "He Will Swallow Up Death in Victory," this verse explains the mechanism of victory: the Servant does not defeat death through might or evasion, but by absorbing its power into himself. His grief and sorrows are not his own but ours. His apparent defeat—appearing stricken by God—is the precise means by which our defeat is reversed. He swallows death by being swallowed by it, and in that seeming annihilation, he transmutes it.

word_study.meaning: to lift up, carry, or sustain; often used in contexts of bearing guilt, iniquity, or burden. The root implies physical or moral carrying.
word_study.significance: This is not mere sympathy or empathy but active substitution. The Servant 'lifts up' and 'carries' our griefs as one might carry a heavy load. This verb will be crucial in verse 12 when Isaiah speaks of the Servant bearing 'the sin of many.' The same word connects suffering to atonement.

word_study.meaning: sickness, weakness, disease, or the pain associated with affliction. Broader in scope than physical illness; can include emotional and spiritual distress.
word_study.significance: The Servant bears not only physical sickness but the entire spectrum of human weakness and suffering. This comprehensive scope indicates that atonement extends to all human infirmities, not merely sin.

word_study.meaning: pains, griefs, emotional and physical suffering. The plural form emphasizes the manifold and varied nature of human suffering.
word_study.significance: By using the plural, Isaiah suggests that the Servant does not bear one generic suffering but the multiplicity of human pains—each specific anguish of each person. This sets the stage for Alma 7:11-13 in the Book of Mormon, where Alma explicitly states that Christ 'shall take upon him the pains and the sicknesses of his people.'

word_study.meaning: touched by affliction or plague; struck down by divine judgment or disease. Often used in contexts of leprosy or ritual impurity.
word_study.significance: The word carries connotations of divine punishment or curse. The irony is precisely that the witnesses misread the Servant's condition as evidence of God's wrath against him, when it is actually God's wrath being borne by him on behalf of others. This is the crux of the Servant's hiddenness: his suffering appears to be retribution, when it is actually redemption.

word_study.meaning: struck, beaten, or smitten. The passive voice emphasizes the Servant as the recipient of blows.
word_study.significance: The Servant is not actively striking back but passively receiving blows. This apparent weakness—the refusal to resist or retaliate—is central to his redemptive power. He absorbs violence rather than perpetuating it.

cross_references.connection: The Book of Mormon quotation of Isaiah 53:4, establishing Nephite understanding that the Messiah would vicariously bear human suffering, not as punishment but as redemptive act.

Alma prophesies that Christ 'shall take upon him the pains and the sicknesses of his people,' directly expanding on Isaiah's doctrine of vicarious suffering to encompass physical infirmities as well as spiritual ones.
Peter applies Isaiah 53:4 to Christ's crucifixion: 'who his own self bare our sins in his own body on the tree,' connecting the Servant's bearing of griefs to the atonement through the cross.

Matthew explicitly cites Isaiah 53:4 in the context of Christ healing the sick, showing that the Servant's bearing of griefs includes bodily infirmities and that healing is part of the redemptive work.

The Lord reveals to Joseph Smith the extent of Christ's suffering in Gethsemane: he 'suffered the pain of all men,' which directly parallels Isaiah's vision of the Servant bearing our griefs and sorrows.

commentary.historical_context: In ancient Israelite thought, suffering was often understood as a consequence of sin—a direct link between transgression and affliction. The Deuteronomic theology prevalent in Israel held that the righteous prospered and the wicked suffered. To assert that a righteous figure would bear the suffering that belonged to others would have been theologically jarring and counterintuitive. The Servant's appearance as 'stricken of God' would have reinforced this conventional judgment: the Servant looks like he is cursed, therefore he must be guilty. Isaiah 53:4 asks the reader to question this equation. The mention of leprosy (implied in 'stricken,' which often refers to plague-struck individuals) would have further reinforced the perception of divine rejection; lepers were ritually unclean and separated from community. Yet Isaiah insists that this very appearance of curse and uncleanness is the mechanism of redemption. This represents a radical reinterpretation of suffering within Israelite theology.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The Book of Mormon explicitly connects Isaiah 53:4 to Nephite teaching about Christ as the Lamb of God. In 1 Nephi 10:10, Nephi speaks of the Lamb of God who 'taketh upon him the sin of the world,' which directly parallels the Servant's bearing of our griefs. Abinadi's sermon in Mosiah 13-15 systematically applies Isaiah 53 to Jesus Christ, teaching that the law of Moses 'had reference to the coming of the Son of God.' The Nephite prophets clearly understood that the Servant passage was not merely consolation literature but prophecy of Christ's specific work.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 19:16-19 contains the most direct modern revelation on this verse. The Lord tells Joseph Smith: 'For behold, I, God, have suffered these things for all, that they might not suffer if they would repent; but if they would not repent they must suffer even as I; which suffering caused myself, even God the greatest of all, to tremble because of pain, and to bleed at every pore, and suffer both body and spirit.' This revelation unpacks the vicarious atonement with unparalleled clarity: Christ bears the suffering so that others need not, contingent on repentance. The phrase 'bleed at every pore' may reference Gethsemane's agony (Luke 22:44) as the locale where the Servant bore our griefs in their fullest weight.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: In temple covenants, members enter covenant relationship with Christ understanding that he has already borne what they could not bear alone. The atonement is the foundation of all temple work; the ordinances are efficacious precisely because Christ satisfied the demands of divine justice. The bearing of griefs is not ceremonial but actual—Christ's literal substitution enables the covenants to have power. Temple patrons who contemplate the atonement while in the temple are directly engaging with the meaning of Isaiah 53:4.

commentary.christological_typology: Isaiah 53:4 establishes Christ as the antitype of all Old Testament sin-bearers and substitutes. The scapegoat of Yom Kippur (Leviticus 16:20-22), who carried away the people's sins into the wilderness, foreshadows the Servant who bears not merely the ceremonial representation of sin but its actual weight. The paschal lamb, whose blood atones for the household, points forward to the Servant as the final Lamb. High priests who bore the iniquities of the nation in the breastplate of judgment (Exodus 28:29-30) are types of the Servant whose bearing is absolute and final. But Isaiah 53:4 transcends these types by presenting a Servant who does not merely represent atonement but embodies it—his person and his work are inseparable. The misinterpretation by witnesses that the Servant is 'stricken of God' reflects the same misunderstanding that disciples initially had at Gethsemane and Golgotha: the appearance of defeat conceals the reality of victory. Only resurrection reveals what the cross means.
commentary.application: For members of The Church of Jesus Christ, Isaiah 53:4 transforms the meaning of personal suffering. When facing grief, sickness, or anguish, the verse offers not an explanation for why suffering exists (theodicy) but a meaning for how it has been redeemed. The Servant has borne our griefs; we do not bear them alone or in vain. This does not mean that faithful members will not suffer—Christ's example proves otherwise—but that suffering is not the final word. More profoundly, the verse invites members into a doctrine of substitution: Christ bore so that we need not bear as he did. His Gethsemane absorbs the full weight of divine justice, making our repentance sufficient for forgiveness. Practically, this verse teaches compassion: if we truly understand that Christ bore our griefs, we are called to bear others' sorrows in a secondary way, becoming instruments of redemption in their lives. The verse also addresses doubt: when the faithful appear to be 'stricken' by circumstance or even by God's apparent silence, Isaiah 53:4 insists that appearance deceives. The very suffering that appears to signal abandonment may be participation in the Servant's redemptive work.

text_kjv: But he was wounded for our transgressions, he was bruised for our iniquities: the chastisement of our peace was upon him; and with his stripes we are healed.

commentary.narrative: This verse crystallizes the substitutionary atonement: the Servant's physical wounding and bruising are explicitly connected to the people's transgressions and iniquities. The word "But" (Hebrew וְאוּלָם ve'ulam) signals a crucial turnabout: despite appearances that the Servant is punished for his own sin (as verse 4 suggested), the reality is precisely opposite—he is wounded for ours. The parallelism is exquisite: "wounded for our transgressions" / "bruised for our iniquities" / "chastisement of our peace was upon him." Each line deepens the substitutionary logic. Most striking is "the chastisement of our peace was upon him"—the punishment that brings us peace is borne by the Servant. Finally, "with his stripes we are healed" shifts from juridical language (punishment for sin) to medical language (restoration of wholeness). The wounds are instruments of healing. For the theme "He Will Swallow Up Death in Victory," this verse explains the cost of victory: death swallows the Servant (his wounding, bruising, and stripes are instruments of death), and in being swallowed by death, he transforms it into the means of healing. His defeat appears total (wounded, bruised, bearing chastisement), yet these very wounds become the source of our restoration. This is the paradox of the atonement: the deepest descent enables the highest ascent.

word_study.meaning: to pierce, wound, or profane. Can also mean to begin or initiate. The root carries connotations of violation and breach.
word_study.significance: The word suggests violent piercing—not incidental bruising but puncturing of the body. When applied to the Servant, it conjures images of lacerations and bleeding. Psalm 22:16 uses related imagery of the pierced sufferer ('they pierced my hands and my feet'), creating a linguistic bridge between Old Testament lament and Isaiah 53's Servant passage.

word_study.meaning: to crush, break, or press down. Often implies complete subjugation or shattering.
word_study.significance: Whereas 'wounded' suggests puncturing wounds, 'bruised' suggests crushing blows—the totality of physical devastation. The Servant is not merely wounded but thoroughly broken. This word appears in Psalm 34:18 ('The Lord is nigh them that are of a broken [bruised] heart'), suggesting that the Servant's crushing is a form of spiritual as well as physical devastation.

word_study.meaning: rebellions, revolts, willful violations of covenant. More than mere mistakes; implies deliberate crossing of established boundaries.
word_study.significance: Transgressions are the gravest category of sin in Hebrew thought—not accidents or ignorances but willful rebellions against God. That the Servant bears these indicates the totality of atonement. Even those who have most deliberately violated covenant are included in the Servant's redemptive work.

word_study.meaning: perversities, crooked or twisted actions, moral distortion. Often carries the sense of guilt or the consequences of sin.
word_study.significance: Whereas 'transgressions' emphasizes the act of crossing boundaries, 'iniquities' emphasize the twisted condition that results from sin. The Servant bears not only our acts but our condition—the warping of our nature that sin produces. This is comprehensive atonement.

word_study.meaning: discipline, correction, or punishment. Often has educational connotations—punishment aimed at reformation.
word_study.significance: The phrase 'the chastisement of our peace' is striking: the discipline that brings us shalom (wholeness, peace, restoration) is borne by the Servant. This inverts typical understanding of punishment: ordinarily, chastisement is something one endures for one's own correction. Here, the Servant endures correction that benefits others. This is the heart of substitutionary atonement.

word_study.meaning: blows, lashes, or wounds inflicted by striking. Often used in contexts of flogging or beating.
word_study.significance: The word conjures images of lashing and beating—the physical instruments of punishment. In Roman context, the stripes would call to mind the scourging Christ endured before crucifixion (Matthew 27:26, Mark 15:15). These are not abstract wounds but literal marks of violence inflicted.

word_study.meaning: to heal, mend, or repair. Can be physical, emotional, or spiritual restoration.
word_study.significance: The shift to medical language ('healed') is crucial. The Servant's wounds become the means of our healing. His stripes do not merely punish him; they restore us. This echoes 1 Peter 2:24, which explicitly applies this verse to Christ's crucifixion as the means of our healing from sin.

cross_references.connection: The Book of Mormon's verbatim quotation of Isaiah 53:5, affirming to Nephite readers that the Messiah's wounding and bruising are redemptive acts for their transgressions and iniquities.

Peter explicitly applies Isaiah 53:5 to Christ's crucifixion: 'by whose stripes ye were healed,' making the wound-healing paradox the foundation of Christian redemption. Peter also connects it to Psalm 23 ('For ye were as sheep going astray'), emphasizing the Servant as the shepherd restoring lost sheep.

Paul teaches that Christ 'was delivered for our offences, and was raised again for our justification,' paralleling Isaiah's structure of substitutionary suffering ('wounded for our transgressions') with resurrection that validates and completes redemption.

Amulek prophesies that the Son of God will 'bring salvation to all those who shall believe on his name' through 'one last sacrifice'—the Servant's ultimate and final atonement work that Isaiah 53:5 describes.

The Lord reveals the extent of Christ's suffering for transgressions and iniquities: he 'suffered the pain of all men,' achieving the substitutionary atonement that Isaiah 53:5 prophesies. The phrase 'bleed at every pore' may indicate the Servant's stripes extending to his entire person.

The author emphasizes that Christ's one sacrifice 'hath perfected for ever them that are sanctified,' connecting the Servant's single atoning act (Isaiah 53:5) to the abolition of all subsequent sacrifices and the completion of redemption.

commentary.historical_context: In the ancient Near Eastern context of sacrifice and substitution, Isaiah 53:5 would have resonated with the logic of Temple sacrifice: an unblemished animal substitutes for the sinner, bearing the penalty of transgression. However, Isaiah extends this logic to a human figure—the Servant—and universalizes it: one person's suffering encompasses the transgressions and iniquities of multitudes. The phrase 'with his stripes we are healed' may draw on ancient Near Eastern ritual texts in which wounding or bloodletting was understood as efficacious for purification and restoration. The substitution of the righteous for the guilty was not unknown in ancient Israel (one thinks of Abraham's willingness to substitute Isaac, or David's offer to bear judgment for his people in 2 Samuel 24:17), but Isaiah 53:5 makes it absolute and final. The verse's emphasis on the Servant's physical wounding (wounded, bruised, stripes) would have been shockingly corporeal to ancient readers: the atonement is not effected through words or ritual but through the actual suffering and bleeding of the Servant's body. This physicality makes the atonement inescapably real and costly.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The entire Nephite understanding of Christ turns on Isaiah 53:5. In 1 Nephi 10:10, Nephi describes the Lamb of God who 'taketh upon him the sin of the world, yea, the sins of every man and woman who hath been, or who shall be, born.' Nephi explicitly extends the Servant's redemption to all humanity, across all time. In 2 Nephi 25:24-26, Nephi teaches that the law of Moses was 'given to point our souls to him' and that 'Christ is the end of the law.' The law's sacrifices all prefigure the Servant's ultimate wounding and bruising. Abinadi (Mosiah 14-15) applies Isaiah 53:5 to Christ's resurrection: the Servant's stripes purchase redemption from death itself. Amulek (Alma 34) adds that the Servant's atonement must be infinite to satisfy the demands of justice—his wounding extends across all souls and all time.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 45:3-5 describes Christ as the 'beginning and the end,' whose atonement encompasses all things. D&C 76:40-42 reveals that Christ's sacrifice benefits even those in the terrestrial kingdom, extending the Servant's redemptive work to the maximum degree. D&C 88:14-16 teaches that Christ is the 'light and the Redeemer of the world'—the source of both physical life and spiritual healing. The Doctrine and Covenants consistently presents the atonement as the central fact of salvation history, validating Isaiah 53:5 as prophecy.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple ceremony places the atonement at the center of covenant life. The covenants made in the temple are possible only because the Servant has borne our transgressions and iniquities. In temple language, the stripes of the Servant are sometimes symbolically represented in the penalties of covenants (in earlier versions of the endowment), which members imposed upon themselves as a sign of consecration to Christ. The symbolism teaches that accepting the atonement means accepting the Servant's wounds as efficacious for one's own healing. The temple also connects Isaiah 53:5 to the healing that comes through ordinances: baptism washes away sin in virtue of the Servant's stripes; the sacrament renews covenant in the light of his sacrifice; higher ordinances seal us to Christ's redemptive work.

commentary.christological_typology: Isaiah 53:5 presents Christ as the ultimate fulfillment of every sacrificial type in the Old Testament. The paschal lamb (Exodus 12:5-7), whose blood protects the firstborn, is fulfilled in Christ's blood poured out for transgressions. The sin offering (Leviticus 4), in which the priest bears the iniquities of the people, is fulfilled in Christ who bears all iniquities. The Servant of Isaiah 53 is simultaneously priest and sacrifice: he effects atonement through his own suffering. The Suffering Servant passage also resonates with the motif of the 'wounded healer' (Jeremiah 30:12-17), where restoration comes through acknowledging and tending to wounds. Most profoundly, Christ fulfills Isaiah 53:5 not metaphorically but literally: he was wounded (pierced at crucifixion), bruised (struck by the soldiers, pressed under the weight of the cross and divine judgment), and bore the chastisement of humanity's peace in Gethsemane and on Golgotha. The stripes of the Roman scourge became the instrument through which the deepest healing—redemption from death and sin—was accomplished.
commentary.application: Isaiah 53:5 is the foundation of personal faith in Christ's atonement. For the individual believer, this verse means that specific sins—not just sins in general—have been borne by the Servant. The transgressions that plague conscience and shame the soul, the iniquities that have twisted one's nature and distorted relationships: these have been brought to the Servant, and he has borne them. The healing promised ('with his stripes we are healed') is not future or contingent but present and assured—it is the heritage of all who believe. More challenging is the verse's implication that one must accept this substitution: the chastisement that should fall on us has been transferred to the Servant. This requires a kind of spiritual humility—the acceptance that we cannot save ourselves, that our transgressions are too grave, our iniquities too deep, for us to remedy. Yet in that humility lies freedom: we are healed not by our own stripes but by his. Practically, Isaiah 53:5 teaches repentance as the reception of substitutionary grace. It is not enough to acknowledge sin; one must turn to the Servant whose wounds heal. For members struggling with guilt, shame, or the weight of past transgression, this verse offers the most direct assurance in scripture: the penalty has been paid, the wound inflicted, the blood shed—not for some future redemption but for us, now. The stripes are already received. Healing is already purchased. The only remaining work is to accept it.

text_kjv: He is brought as a lamb to the slaughter, and as a sheep before her shearers is dumb, so he openeth not his mouth.

commentary.narrative:
This verse stands at the emotional and theological center of Isaiah's Suffering Servant prophecy—a passage the early Church explicitly identified as Christ (see Acts 8:32–35). The image of a lamb led to slaughter appears deceptively simple on the surface: a docile animal moving toward death without resistance or protest. But the context transforms it into something far more profound. Isaiah is describing not helplessness but submission—a voluntary surrender of power in the face of injustice. The "dumbness" here is not muteness born of inability to speak, but silence born of choice. Christ could have called twelve legions of angels (Matthew 26:53), could have retaliated with divine power, could have defended himself verbally at his trial. Instead, he remained silent. This silence is the ultimate expression of the "swallowing up of death in victory"—not through military conquest or aggressive self-defense, but through the acceptance of suffering itself as the redemptive act.

For Isaiah's original audience, the lamb imagery would have resonated with the Temple sacrifice system they knew intimately. Every Passover lamb, every sin offering, every daily burnt offering pointed toward this moment. The Hebrew people understood that covenant relationship with God often required sacrifice, submission, and trust in divine purposes beyond human comprehension. Yet none of those rituals had ever been performed by the victim voluntarily—they were brought by others. Here Isaiah describes something unprecedented: a willing victim who goes to the altar understanding fully what awaits, choosing silence over self-preservation, choosing obedience over vindication.

The phrase "brought as a lamb" (נִשְׁמַט כַּשֶּׂה לַטָּבַח—nishmat kasseh latavach) uses passive voice, suggesting that while Christ is brought by others, he is brought *as* a lamb—he embodies the role, accepts the position, makes it his own. The verb "is brought" (נִשְׁמַט) can also carry the sense of being taken or handed over, which Matthew and Mark use when describing Judas's betrayal. What began as betrayal by human hands becomes, in Isaiah's vision, the fulfillment of God's redemptive plan. The second image—"as a sheep before her shearers is dumb"—adds another layer. A sheep being sheared experiences violation, exposure, loss, yet remains silent not from dignity alone but from the nature of sheep themselves. They do not resist because they cannot comprehend the purpose. But Christ, fully conscious, chooses what the sheep cannot: to understand and accept the stripping away of everything for the sake of others' salvation.

word_study.meaning: A young sheep, specifically a lamb used in sacrifice. The term appears 99 times in the Hebrew Bible, predominantly in sacrificial contexts (Exodus 12, Leviticus 1–7). It denotes both the literal animal and, by extension, innocence, vulnerability, and prescribed ritual.
word_study.significance: John the Baptist's identification of Jesus as "the Lamb of God, which taketh away the sin of the world" (John 1:29) directly echoes this verse. In the Restoration, the lamb is central to covenant theology—the Doctrine and Covenants emphasizes that Christ is 'the Lamb slain from the foundation of the world' (D&C 76:39). The term carries the full weight of Passover redemption theology and the daily Temple sacrifice system.

word_study.term_original: יִלְמַד (yilmad) — though the KJV reads "is dumb," the Hebrew actually uses the niphal form suggesting muteness or silence
word_study.meaning: Silent, mute, unable or unwilling to speak. The root carries the sense of being speechless in the face of injustice or suffering. It is not the inability to speak, but the choice or state of remaining silent despite having grounds for protest or defense.
word_study.significance: Matthew 26:63 records that when the high priest adjured Jesus to say whether he was the Messiah, 'Jesus held his peace'—a deliberate silence in the face of accusation. This was extraordinary: any accused person had every incentive to defend himself. Christ's silence becomes an act of redemptive submission, fulfilling this prophecy. In later temple symbolism, the silence of the sacrificial victim becomes central to covenant language about yielding one's life.

word_study.meaning: To slaughter, kill, butcher—the violent taking of life, typically of sacrificial animals. The term appears in both literal sacrificial contexts and metaphorical contexts describing judgment and death.
word_study.significance: This is not gentle death but violent death—the cross was an instrument of torture and shame. Isaiah does not soften the reality of what awaits the Servant. The crucifixion was, to the ancient mind, the death of a criminal and a slave, the most shameful end possible. That the Messiah would meet such a death directly contradicted Jewish expectations of a triumphant, conquering king. Yet Isaiah prepares the faithful for this paradox: death and victory are not opposites in God's economy; the Servant's death *is* the victory.

cross_references.connection: When the high priest asks if Jesus is the Messiah, 'Jesus held his peace.' This fulfills Isaiah's prophecy of silence—not inability to speak, but voluntary restraint in the face of accusation.

Peter applies this verse directly to Christ: 'Who, when he was reviled, reviled not again; when he suffered, he threatened not; but committed himself to him that judgeth righteously.' The silent suffering becomes an example for believers.

Philip uses this exact verse to teach the Ethiopian eunuch about Jesus, confirming that the early Church identified the Suffering Servant as Christ and used Isaiah 53:7 as direct Christological proof text.

John the Baptist's declaration that Jesus is 'the Lamb of God, which taketh away the sin of the world' directly fulfills the lamb imagery in this verse, identifying Jesus as the ultimate sacrificial victim.

Modern revelation identifies Christ as 'the Lamb slain from the foundation of the world,' confirming that his sacrificial role was predetermined and central to God's redemptive plan before mortality began.

commentary.historical_context: In ancient Israel, the Temple sacrifice system was the primary mode of atonement and covenant renewal. Multiple categories of sacrifice existed—the burnt offering, the sin offering, the peace offering, the grain offering—each with prescribed animals and procedures detailed in Leviticus. The lamb (specifically a yearling male lamb without blemish) was the standard victim for daily burnt offerings and the Passover sacrifice. Crucially, the victim was *brought* by the worshipper; the animal did not choose to be sacrificed. It went to the altar because it lacked volition. Isaiah's prophecy introduces a profound innovation: the Servant, fully conscious and possessing complete power, chooses to go as a willing victim. This reverses the fundamental dynamic of all prior sacrifice. Additionally, crucifixion in the Roman world was not a Jewish form of execution—it was a shameful pagan death reserved for slaves, rebels, and the worst criminals. That the Messiah would die by crucifixion was, to the Jewish mind, a scandal and contradiction. Isaiah prepares the believing community to recognize that God's redemptive plan moves outside normal categories of honor and shame, strength and weakness, triumph and defeat.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Mosiah 14:7 reproduces this verse identically, preserving it for the Nephite believers. Abinadi, in teaching Isaiah's Suffering Servant passage, emphasizes that Christ 'cometh to his people, and all those who believe on his name shall be saved' (Mosiah 13:33), reframing the sacrifice as redemptive rather than merely punitive. The Book of Mormon context makes clear that the willing suffering of the Servant is inseparable from universal salvation.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 19:16–19 contains Christ's own description of his suffering: 'For behold, I, God, have suffered these things for all, that they might not suffer if they would repent.' The voluntariness of Christ's suffering is central—he suffers so that others need not. This voluntary submission transforms suffering from punishment into redemption. D&C 45:3–5 also emphasizes Christ as the Lamb who 'taketh away the sins of the world,' linking the Servant theology of Isaiah to restored temple and covenant language.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: In the temple endowment, the theme of covenant sacrifice and willing submission appears throughout. The Lamb of God imagery in Isaiah 53:7 informs covenant language about laying down one's life for principle and faith. The silence of the Suffering Servant becomes a model for the silence observed in sacred ordinances—not enforced muteness, but sacred discretion born of understanding and reverence.

commentary.christological_typology: Isaiah 53:7 presents Christ as the ultimate fulfillment of the entire sacrificial system of ancient Israel. Every lamb brought to the Temple altar foreshadows this lamb—but with a crucial difference. All prior sacrifices were involuntary on the part of the victim; this sacrifice is entirely voluntary. Christ embodies what no previous sacrifice could: a victim who goes willingly, with full knowledge and power to resist, choosing submission to God's will and humanity's redemption over self-preservation. The 'dumbness' of the Servant reverses expected patterns of power and vindication. Normally, the strong defend themselves, the innocent protest their punishment, the righteous demand justice. Christ does none of these. His silence is not weakness but the ultimate expression of power—power exercised not to save himself but to save others. In Jewish thought, the Suffering Servant passages describe what is often called the 'Messiah ben Joseph'—a suffering, dying messiah distinct from the triumphant 'Messiah ben David.' Isaiah resolves this paradox: the Servant's suffering and death *are* the victory. Death is not defeat but the weapon by which sin and death itself are overcome. 'He will swallow up death in victory' (Isaiah 25:8) because he, the Lamb, freely surrenders to death—and in so doing, transforms it.
commentary.application: For the modern believer approaching Easter, Isaiah 53:7 invites profound reflection on the nature of power and redemption. We live in a culture that equates power with the ability to dominate, to win arguments, to defend oneself, to come out on top. Christ's example here—brought as a lamb, silent before accusers, divested of all earthly dignity and defense—presents a radically different model. The message is not that passivity is always correct or that injustice should go unchallenged, but that there are times when the greatest victory comes not from assertion of self but from submission to a larger purpose. In covenant life, members are invited into this same pattern: to 'lay down' their natural inclinations, their need for vindication, their demand to be understood or appreciated, and to trust that in yielding to God's will—even when it costs—they participate in redemption. The Servant's silence also challenges us to examine our own words. How often do we speak in self-defense when silence would serve better? How often do we justify ourselves when we might instead reflect and listen? The silence of Christ before the high priest and before Pilate is not evasion but clarity—he had already spoken his truth; further argument would change nothing. Easter invites us to that same clarity: to understand what is truly essential, and to have the courage to submit to what matters most, even when it requires the sacrifice of what the world values.

text_kjv: And he made his grave with the wicked, and with the rich in his death; although he had done no violence, neither was any deceit in his mouth.

commentary.narrative:
Isaiah 53:9 marks a turning point in the suffering servant passage—the moment where injustice reaches its apex and becomes the platform for vindication. The servant is buried among criminals and the wealthy, a dual humiliation that speaks to both condemnation and attempted erasure. Yet the verse's second half arrests this trajectory: "although he had done no violence, neither was any deceit in his mouth." This parenthetical assertion of innocence is crucial. Isaiah is not merely describing physical arrangement of bodies; he is declaring that the servant's placement among the wicked is a miscarriage of justice, not a reflection of guilt. The rich may claim a share in his grave through their investment in his death (as verse 9 continues in context), but they cannot claim a share in his actual culpability.

For the Easter theme "He Will Swallow Up Death in Victory," this verse is essential: it shows that death has done its worst—the innocent condemned, the righteous buried in dishonor—and yet this defeat becomes the foundation of resurrection and exaltation. The servant's death is not redemptive because it is deserved, but because it is *undeserved*. His innocence makes his voluntary sacrifice an act of infinite atoning power. The grave that was meant to silence him becomes the threshold of his triumph. Death attempted to swallow the servant; instead, the servant will swallow up death in victory.

word_study.meaning: burial place, sepulcher; by extension, the realm of death and finality. In Hebrew thought, the grave represents not merely a physical location but the ultimate endpoint of earthly existence and the seeming victory of death over life.
word_study.significance: The choice of qāver rather than שְׁאוֹל (sheol, the underworld) emphasizes the physical, visible, shameful reality of burial among the wicked. Yet for the Latter-day Saint reader, the grave is also the place of resurrection—death's domain becomes the stage for its defeat.

word_study.meaning: the guilty, the lawless, those in rebellion against God. The term denotes moral culpability and covenant violation.
word_study.significance: The servant's placement with reshāʿim highlights the scandal of his condemnation. He is grouped with those deserving death, yet he alone is innocent—a reversal that becomes the template for all subsequent redemption.

word_study.meaning: wealthy, prosperous; in prophetic literature often paired with power and, implicitly, complicity in injustice.
word_study.significance: The rich do not merely bury him—they 'possess' or 'divide' his grave (depending on translation tradition; the Hebrew דִּבְרוֹ can mean 'his word/saying' or imply possession). They attempt to claim him as one of their victims, a trophy of their power.

word_study.meaning: violence, wrong, injustice, violation of covenant. More than mere physical brutality; it denotes a rupture of the moral and social order.
word_study.significance: The servant's complete absence of chāmās stands in stark contrast to the wicked and the rich who surround his grave. His innocence of violence mirrors his innocence of deceit—he violates no law, sacred or civil.

word_study.meaning: deceit, treachery, falsehood; a breach of trust and authenticity.
word_study.significance: In ancient Near Eastern thought, the mouth was the locus of covenant fidelity. A mouth free of mirmāh is a mouth that keeps covenant absolutely. For Christians, this prophesies Christ's absolute truthfulness; for Latter-day Saints, it prefigures the servant's divine integrity and capacity to atone.

cross_references.connection: Peter applies this verse directly to Jesus: 'Who did no sin, neither was guile found in his mouth.' The New Testament interprets Isaiah's servant as Christ, grounding this prophecy in historical fulfillment.
The Book of Mormon preserves Isaiah 53:9 in the mouth of Abinadi, making it a Nephite testimony to Christ's innocence and the injustice of his condemnation centuries before the meridian of time.

Joseph of Arimathea, a rich man, takes the body of Jesus and places it in his own new tomb—a literal fulfillment of 'he made his grave with the rich in his death,' yet also a sign that even the wealthy cannot truly 'own' the Christ or prevent his resurrection.

Paul's declaration that death is 'swallowed up in victory' directly echoes Isaiah's theme; the servant's innocent death becomes the instrument by which death itself is defeated and rendered powerless.
Amulek teaches that Christ will 'bring to pass the resurrection of the dead,' reversing the finality of the grave and proving that innocent death, freely given, has atoning power beyond itself.

commentary.historical_context: In ancient Near Eastern context, burial with the wicked was a form of shame and disenfranchisement. Proper burial with one's ancestors was essential to honor and continuity; improper burial was tantamount to being cast out of the covenant community. The mention of 'the rich' alongside 'the wicked' reflects a cultural reality in which the wealthy often wielded judicial and coercive power, and could conspire against the innocent with impunity. The Suffering Servant passage inverts the expected order: the one buried as a criminal is the truly innocent one, while his condemners—wicked and rich alike—perpetrate injustice. This inversion would have been shocking to an ancient Israelite audience, who would have expected innocence to be vindicated in life, not only retrospectively through resurrection. The verse also reflects ancient Near Eastern concepts of the grave as final and irrevocable—yet Isaiah's prophetic assertion of the servant's innocence suggests that even the grave cannot hold the innocent.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Abinadi's quotation of this verse in Mosiah 14:9 situates it within a Book of Mormon narrative of righteous suffering and vindication. Abinadi himself is burned to death for his testimony, much like the servant is condemned despite innocence. The Book of Mormon thus reads Isaiah 53:9 not as ancient prophecy alone, but as a pattern that repeats: righteous prophets and servants are condemned, yet their innocence and their sacrifice carry eternal weight. This invites Latter-day Saints to see themselves within this pattern.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 76:70-80 describes the celestial kingdom and the exaltation available to all who come to Christ. The servant's innocent death and subsequent victory become the template for all who overcome death: their graves, too, are sites not of final defeat but of resurrection. D&C 88:14-16 teaches that 'the spirit and the body shall be reunited again in its perfect form; both and spirit and element, inseparably connected, receiveth a fulness of joy' — a promise made possible by the servant's swallowing up of death in victory.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: In temple theology, the servant's burial and resurrection mirror the death and rebirth symbolism of the endowment. The grave becomes a passageway, not a prison. The servant's innocence and integrity make him the worthy representative through whom all may pass. The temple itself—as a restored house of covenants—is built on the foundation of the servant's atonement and resurrection; it is the place where the faithful enact and claim the victory over death that the servant's sacrifice secured.

commentary.christological_typology: Isaiah 53:9 is dense with Christological significance. The servant's burial with the wicked prophesies Christ's crucifixion between thieves and his placement in a criminal's grave (from the perspective of those who condemned him). His burial with 'the rich' is fulfilled in Joseph of Arimathea's tomb—a detail that Matthew's gospel explicitly notes as a fulfillment of Isaiah 53 (Matt. 27:57-60). More profoundly, the servant's innocence in the face of condemnation makes him the only being capable of atoning for the world's guilt. His death is not payment for his own transgressions (he had none) but a voluntary offering for all humanity's transgressions. This is the core of Christological typology: the Messiah must be innocent to represent the innocent and to represent all who repent and come to him. The 'grave with the wicked' becomes paradoxically the site of redemption, because the innocent one occupies it. For Latter-day Saints, this also prefigures the resurrection, which for all of Adam's descendants depends on the innocent servant's victory over death.
commentary.application: For modern covenant members, Isaiah 53:9 teaches a profound truth about suffering and innocence. It is possible to do all things well, to walk in integrity, and still be condemned by the world. The verse does not promise that innocence will be vindicated in this life; rather, it asserts that innocence has ultimate, eternal weight. The servant's grave does not define him; his resurrection does. For members enduring unjust treatment—whether by family, society, or circumstance—this verse offers perspective: your innocence and integrity matter to God, regardless of how the world arranges your circumstances. Like the servant, your vindication may come not in the moment but in the resurrection. Additionally, the verse invites reflection on complicity: the 'rich' and the 'wicked' who seal the servant's grave are not abstract forces but deliberate agents. This calls modern members to examine whether they are, in any way, complicit in systems that condemn the innocent or that exalt the wealthy over the righteous. Easter, the triumph over death, is built on the foundation of the servant's innocent death—and that victory is available to all who, like the servant, choose integrity over expediency.

text_kjv: Therefore will I divide him a portion with the great, and he shall divide the spoil with the strong; because he hath poured out his soul unto death: and he was numbered with the transgressors; and he bare the sins of many, and made intercession for the transgressors.

commentary.narrative: Isaiah 53:12 stands as the triumphant conclusion to the Suffering Servant passage, the capstone of Israel's greatest messianic prophecy. After four verses depicting the Servant's rejection, suffering, and death, this final verse pivots decisively to vindication and exaltation. The opening word 'Therefore' marks a dramatic turning point: because He poured out His soul unto death—precisely because of His complete sacrifice—God will exalt Him to share spoils like a warrior king. This is the promise that swallows up death in victory. The 'great' and the 'strong' refer to the mighty and powerful of the earth; the Servant will sit among them as an equal, not as a vanquished victim. For Latter-day Saints reading this during Easter week, this verse encapsulates the Atonement's dual work: the price paid (soul poured out, numbered with transgressors, bearing sins) and the reward earned (division of spoils, exaltation, eternal intercession).

word_study.meaning: to divide, apportion, distribute—often used of dividing spoils or inheritance. The verb suggests not just receiving a portion, but being formally allocated a share by God's decree.
word_study.significance: The language echoes Psalm 49:17 and military victory imagery. God Himself is the one who divides and assigns; this is not the Servant's self-exaltation but divine vindication and reward.

word_study.meaning: literally, to expose, bare, or pour out one's life/soul. 'Soul' (נַפְשׁ, nephesh) here means the whole person, life force, or inner self. The verb conveys complete self-emptying and self-sacrifice.
word_study.significance: This echoes Philippians 2:7 concept of kenosis (self-emptying). For LDS readers, this language reflects the Savior's complete surrender in Gethsemane and on Calvary—not a partial offering but total outpouring of self. The phrase connects to D&C 88:6 and the theme of Christ giving His life.

word_study.meaning: to be counted, reckoned, or included among. 'Transgressors' (פּוֹשְׁעִים, posheim) are those who rebel or act wickedly. The Servant is tallied, census-taken, grouped with sinners.
word_study.significance: This fulfills the paradox of the Atonement: the Innocent One identified with the guilty. Luke 22:37 explicitly applies this verse to Jesus being crucified between two thieves. It underscores vicarious substitution—He takes the sinner's place, number, and shame.

word_study.meaning: to lift up, carry, bear—often used of bearing guilt or punishment. The parallelism with 'poured out his soul' and 'made intercession' shows this is active, ongoing, redemptive bearing, not passive suffering. 'Many' (רַבִּים, rabbim) likely means 'the many' as corporate humanity.
word_study.significance: This is the core vocabulary of Levitical sacrifice and Israelite theology of atonement. The Servant does not merely suffer; He bears away sin as a priest bears the burden of the nation. Alma 7:13 quotes this directly, and D&C 45:4 echoes it. This bearing is not just past-tense (Gethsemane and Calvary) but eternal—'made intercession' (present/ongoing).

word_study.meaning: to encounter, meet, intervene, or intercede. Literally, 'to fall upon' or 'to place oneself between.' Used of interceding before a king or pleading a case.
word_study.significance: This verb places the Servant in the eternal high priestly role. Isaiah does not say 'will have made intercession' (past) but uses a participial form suggesting continuous, eternal action. This connects directly to Hebrews 7:25 and D&C 45:3-5, where Christ's intercession is ongoing. For Latter-day Saints, this echoes temple theology: the Savior stands forever in the presence of the Father, advocating for the sins of the world.

cross_references.connection: The fulfillment of Isaiah 53:12—Jesus explicitly affirmed this verse applied to Him: 'He was reckoned among the transgressors.' This verse was read at the Last Supper as Jesus explained His imminent passion.

The eternal intercession of Christ: 'He ever liveth to make intercession for them.' Isaiah 53:12's 'made intercession for the transgressors' is the Old Testament foundation for the New Testament doctrine of Christ's perpetual high priestieship.

Book of Mormon explicitly quotes Isaiah 53:12 verbatim: the Savior 'shall poured out his soul unto death' and 'bare the sins of many.' Alma applies this directly to the pre-mortal covenant between Christ and Heavenly Father.

The Savior declares His dual role—suffering unto death and eternal intercession: 'I came into the world to do the will of my Father, because my Father sent me. And my Father sent me that I might be lifted up upon the cross; and that I might draw all men unto me.' This is the operative theology of Isaiah 53:12.

The triumph over death: 'Death is swallowed up in victory' directly echoes the resurrection victory that Isaiah 53:12's vindication anticipates. The Atonement's completion in the Resurrection is the answer to 'He will swallow up death in victory.'

Messianic parallel: 'God will redeem my soul from the power of the grave.' The vindication and exaltation motif of Isaiah 53:12 ('divide him a portion with the great') mirrors the psalmist's confidence in resurrection and elevation.

commentary.historical_context: Isaiah 53 draws on multiple Old Testament traditions: the Suffering Servant songs (Isaiah 42, 49, 50, 52-53), the scapegoat ritual (Leviticus 16), the guilt offering (Leviticus 5), and royal davidic messianism. By the 1st century, Jewish messianic expectation was fractured: some awaited a conquering messiah-king; others, especially after the Maccabean era, contemplated a suffering messiah. The Dead Sea Scrolls and later rabbinic literature show divided interpretation of Isaiah 53—some applied it to the righteous remnant, others to a future messiah. The cultural background of 'dividing spoil' draws on ancient Near Eastern military practice: victorious kings apportioned conquered wealth and status among their warriors. For Jews in Jesus's time, 'numbered with transgressors' had specific legal implications—one who was executed or crucified was deemed cursed and separated from the covenant community (Deuteronomy 21:23). The Servant's vindication thus meant not just personal restoration but covenantal reintegration and triumph.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Alma 7:13 reproduces Isaiah 53:12 as the Savior's own testimony of His pre-mortal covenant with Heavenly Father.
